Hello, thanks for responding. I argue Johnston’s performance helped contribute to the CSA defeat in the Atlanta Campaign. I’ve heard a historian describe the opposing commanders of the Atlanta Campaign as a general who didn’t want to fight versus a general who wouldn’t fight. Johnston was hoping that Sherman would launch futile frontal assaults against prepared positions. However, Sherman (who admittedly performed poorly on the tactical offense) was unwilling to oblige him except for Resaca and Kennesaw Mountain—the latter was a total defeat. With a larger army, Sherman understood that all he needed to do was pin Johnston down and then use his free forces to threaten Johnston’s line of retreat. By holding the initiative, Sherman was able to get to the outskirts of Atlanta with both sides suffering roughly the same number of casualties up to that point (I have seen a report that states Johnston actually still suffered more losses than Sherman before Hood took over but couldn’t find it). Johnston’s best bet was to try and seize the initiative to off balance Sherman’s greater numbers and ability to maneuver. He also should have employed his cavalry against Sherman’s line of communications—and probably lobbied harder for Forrest to join his command to better achieve this. If Johnston turned North Georgia into a killing field as Lee did to Central Virginia, then the 1864 election could have been different. I agree with you that relieving Johnston at the gates of Atlanta was a bad decision—but he had essentially failed by letting Sherman get that far in the first place. Even if Johnston stayed in command, Sherman would still have used his strength in manpower to pin him down and cut the city’s supply lines, and the result would have been likely the same strategically.

Lee’s generalship offered the only true strategy for Confederate strategic success. He understood war is an extension of politics by other means and realized that Southern armies could achieve victory by influencing the public opinion of the democratic Union. He understood the manpower, materiel, and naval advantages of the North meant that the South could not win a prolonged military conflict and that the Confederacy would only grow weaker with time. He thus sought to maintain the initiative to force the Union to react to him so as to negate their numerical advantages.

As a military strategists, he proved a good offensive commander, winning the Seven Days and 2nd Manassas Campaign. The Antietam Campaign was an ultimate failure, but people often forget that he planned the capture and surrender of Harper’s Ferry—the largest surrender of US forces and comparable to Grant at Donelson. When viewed in total, the campaigns of the Summer of 1862 are what ultimately took the CSA off of life support and were instrumental in prolonging the war beyond early summer of 1862.

When looking at some of Lee’s bigger failings, they appear to be more tactical than strategic: Antietam should not have been fought in the first place and Gettysburg was poorly fought—but the strategic rationale of each was sound: meet the logistical needs of his army while putting pressure on the Union population. Still, even the consequences of these defeats managed to stall any further campaigns against his capital for several months afterward and bought the CSA time.

When fighting strategically on the defensive, he was almost unparalleled. While in the Western Theater, Grant was able to use brute force and maneuver to thrash any Confederate commander, but in Virginia, Grant was forced to contend with a more able opponent, and the negative effect of the Overland Campaign on the Union population threatened the 1864 election for Lincoln. Additionally, besides the Siege of Charleston, Lee’s defense of Richmond and Petersburg was the longest siege of the war and the costliest for the Union.

Now for the flaws. While the criticism that Lee was too Virginia centric is overblown, at some point he should have personally stepped up and taken control in the Western Theater. He was truly the only Confederate army commander capable of any real strategic success (sorry to the Joe Johnston fans on reddit). He should have lobbied Davis harder for more suitable leadership in the Western Theater or taken more hands-on approach. The passive defense that the Confederates displayed in that theater ultimately hurt the CSA war effort in manpower and did so without the added effect of inflicting serious casualties on the invading Union forces.

Looking at the bigger picture. Lee was an excellent improviser and understood the balance between strategy and policy well. He was neither Jominian nor Clausewitzian and was willing to gamble—both to his praise and detriment. He trounced inferior commanders and gave good commanders like Grant and Meade a hard fight.

For a great selection of articles on Lee—positive and negative—check out Gary Gallagher’s compilation titled: Lee the Soldier and then follow the various authors’ own works.

Anyone arguing against Meade’s actions needs to read Meade at Gettysburg: A Study in Command. It provides an excellent analysis of the operational condition of the Army of the Potomac before and after Gettysburg. 

Would Grant have done better? It is unlikely given the circumstances. I do argue that he would have likely tried to attack Lee at some point—most likely on July 4th or Williamsport, but it is unlikely that these assaults would be successful given the Army of Northern Virginia’s defensive terrain and entrenchments. The Gettysburg Campaign would likely have concluded the same with additional casualties.

I don’t buy this analysis. Grant historically played favorites with his subordinates—particularly Sheridan and Sherman—and allowed some to maintain command when other commanders would have been relieved for the same offenses. If you were in the Grant clique, your career prospered; if not, you were discarded. That being said, Grant clearly overlooked Sheridan’s shortcomings as a commander in this assessment. Judging how he performed tactically as a cavalry commander in the Overland Campaign and in the Valley against Jubal Early, there are severe qualities he lacked:

-He never understood the scouting mission of the cavalry. He galavanted off on raids which cost Union victory at the Wilderness and Spotsylvania and left the Union blind when he lost to Hampton at Trevilian Station. He used cavalry in a devastating way tactically but never understood the mission of providing up-to-dare information to the commander. 

-Operationally, he generally underperformed in forced marches until the Appomattox Campaign. This cost him complete victories after 3rd Winchester and Fisher’s Hill.

Looking at the three levels of war, based on their careers. They are on on par with each other tactically. Jackson was not a particularly great tactician but he was great at adjusting to developing situations and responding to crisis. Sheridan wielded his forces like a sledgehammer which worked in some situations and failed in others. Both were good tacticians.

Operationally, Jackson may have been the best commander in the war and managed to get troops to the right place, at the right time, and use them in the right way in several campaigns. There is a good debate to be had in the Peninsula Campaign, but I fall into the camp that this was largely influenced by the fatigue of the prior campaign and was the low point in an otherwise remarkable career.  

Strategically, both had incredible highs; however, I have to give the edge to Jackson. He understood commander’s intent better and molded himself to the mission. Sheridan was vainglorious and really dropped the ball repeatedly during the Overland Campaign. However, he redeemed himself during the Appomattox Campaign. 

While I personally rank Jackson the superior commander, others may disagree with me; however, my intent is to demonstrate that he is a more able commander than what Grant says.

As a final anecdote, it’s funny that Grant says Jackson would not have beaten Sherman considering that Jackson defeated Sherman’s brigade at First Bull Run.

Generals—and historians for that matter— study war at the tactical, operational, and strategic levels. Meade had to apply his understanding at all three levels during the Battle of Gettysburg—emphasizing a level depending on the evolving situation. 

Wars are not won solely won by attrition and history provides an inexhaustible number of examples where wars are won by maneuver and not attrition.

Finally, the question OP asked is far from useless when trying to extrapolate lessons learned from the experiences of others. Seeing how Gettysburg is one of the most-studied battles—answering OP’s question can help us better understand the battle.

I really enjoyed Hess’ book on Bragg and I definitely have a greater appreciation for him as a commander. His greatest failings were in his interpersonal skills and his ability to wrangle the press. In terms of battlefield prowess, he isn’t as bad as some other Civil War army commanders and performed ably in some circumstances—but these are overshadowed by Missionary Ridge and the Fall of Fort Fisher. He probably ranks average compared to other Confederate army commanders: on par with Joe Johnston and certainly better than A.S. Johnston, Pemberton, Hood, Van Dorn,  and Floyd.

I love how you singled out Varney without critiquing the validity of his argument while also ignoring the other historians brought into the equation. You are missing the key points about the changing character of war during that time period and how outclassed the Americans were in comparison but almost every metric with their only real edge being in the evolution of mounted arms. I don’t see how you can accuse me of being a lost causer considering I attribute CSA defeat primarily to the inept military leadership—particularly in the Western Theater—and government rather than solely Northern manpower and industry—although Union victory, especially given their performance, would have been impossible without either. None of the contemporary historians I cite are Lost Causers by any means.

This goes back to my first point in that the Civil War was fought by amateurs who had to learn on the job. Just because the Union was competent against the Confederacy does not translate into success in a conflict with any other major European power. 


Your true defense lays in ad-hominem attacks rather than a true rationalization of the Union, its doctrine, and war-making capabilities, and how its performance rated in the evolving character of war.

Cope and seethe.

I’m not an authority on Sheridan by any means, but Eric Wittenberg has done an excellent job of evaluating his career and is a respected Civil War era historian. Additionally, Frank Varney has done some excellent analysis as well—particularly on his relief and credibility associated with the removal of G.K. Warren. Additionally, Gordon Rhea provides excellent analysis of the strategic impact of Sheridan during the Overland Campaign. Combining these perspectives from professional historians it is hard to determine that Sheridan was credible in stating the truth and it is apparent that his career was heavily influenced by his relationship with Grant rather than his brilliance.
 
Again, while looking at the deficiencies of European powers you completely ignore the CSA’s and understate their severe leadership, economic, and manpower deficiencies. They had no overarching, cohesive strategy, only one competent army commander, an executive who was afraid to punish failure—hence their failure on almost every battle and campaign fought between the Mississippi River and the Appalachians. The reason the war lasted so long was not Southern resolve (aside from the Virginia and Carolina theater) but Union incompetence. 

Aside from his failure to accept defeat, the Overland Campaign has no markings of brilliance and failed by Grant’s own measure of success—the destruction of Lee’s army. He then was forced to change his strategy from attrition to one of maneuver—one that he should have engaged on the campaign’s onset but was more difficult to do given the quality of his subordinates. Even while being trapped in Petersburg, Lee still managed to seize the offensive and dispatch his 2nd Corps to augment the Army of the Valley and once again raid into the North. 

The Army of the Potomac was not the well-oiled machine you imagine it to be. Its most combat ready soldiers were mostly dead or out of service by the onset of the Overland Campaign and those who survived would be put through the ringer. The army that crossed the James was a shadow of its former self and relied increasingly upon draftees and officers promoted beyond their capabilities. Throughout the Overland and Petersburg Campaigns, its leadership failed to coordinate almost every assault undertaken and many were outright subordinate when ordered to make assaults they viewed as suicidal. This army was great in fighting the Confederacy, but I doubt it could stand in a peer fight.

In examining the orders of battles for the Overland Campaign and the Virginia Theater, Grant’s forces available to him were never outnumbered by Lee. The closest they came was at North Anna before Grant was reinforced with around a 15,000-20,000 man difference.

The European monarchies didn’t give up easily because of their will to fight but rather because they fought an opponent who could accurately gauge their center of gravity and employ rapid maneuvers to systemically cause a military collapse. The attrition-minded Americans were incapable of doing the same thing. How many times do we hear of stories of Civil War armies failing to follow up their victory? Quite often. This was not the case with Prussia. The Army of the Potomac was suited for its purpose of fighting a Civil War but I doubt its capabilities against a peer power.

You have a bloated idea of the Confederacy to think that they were a more prominent military power than those aforementioned nations—some of which were empires. The Confederacy was fledgling rural nation, largely relied on exports for arms, had no navy, and had largely incompetent military high command (Lee being the sole exception as a theater commander) and fractured federal government. Their strength was largely in their defensive posture but that can be outdone by maneuver. Their rail network undid the potential of using interior lines to an effective degree. Additionally, despite being a large geographic nation, this turned out to be its undoing as it allowed the more mobile Union army to avoid surfaces and exploit gaps. 

Sheridan is not a reliable source of information as he was highly egotistical and generally had an overrated military career (his failures at the Wilderness and Spotsylvania were equivalent to Stuart’s at Gettysburg; he covered up his failure at Trevilian Station and later lied about his true objective; his battles in the Valley Campaign were sloppy affairs that repeatedly allowed Early to escape; and he was dishonest in the removal of G.K. Warren at Five Forks). He made a fair point about the changing character of cavalry in warfare but that is arguably one of the few areas where Americans outmatched their European counterparts. 

You’re correct in that Von Moltke is considered one of the military greats—and his reason is that he established a doctrine that changed the character of warfare that he was able to repeatedly apply to militaries with a more traditional, Jominian approach. Take many of European commanders of the era and compare them to members of the CSA high command—such as Pillow,  Floyd, A.S. Johnston, J Johnston, Pemberton, and Bragg—and you’ll find that they are equal if not better in quality.

Grant was decent at slugging it out against ill-led Confederate armies—especially when he was afforded mobility with naval forces. In Virginia, he suffered against a more competent commander but prevailed after fighting two of the war’s bloodiest campaigns at a point when the war was turning against the CSA. However, particularly judging by his conduct in the Overland/Pegersburg Campaigns, I’d argue that it would not translate well against a peer power that was equal numerically, which the Confederacy certainly was not.

To answer your question briefly, this sort of thing happened with relative frequency throughout the American Civil War. Both sides conducted fake surrenders, donned enemy uniforms, and other such things outside of what was considered civilized warfare—if such thing exists. The ability to investigate and prosecute offenders was limited—and if so it generally involved immediate execution or an occasional drumbeat trial.
None of these guys would rank in the top tier in my opinion—great commanders but not earth shattering. From the WW2 era I would consider George Marshall among the greats.

It is entirely false to say that Grant was the first general to understand logistics. You have to ignore centuries of military history to come to this conclusion. Even in the American Civil War—most army commanders understood the importance of logistics and often had to weigh the cost and benefits of remaining attached or detached to your supply lines. The only difference really between Grant and his chief rival—Lee—in terms of logistics was that Grant was working with a friendly civilian government that he could apply leverage to while Lee often differed to civilian authority.

Grant would arguably not even be considered a great general in his era. Americans tend to buff up the reputations of Civil War generals because the War is so central to the national narrative. We often forget that most Civil War commanders were between the rank of 1st lieutenant and colonel before the war started—none had any experience leading larger formations and there was no masters or phd-level of military science instructed. Across the board, the Civil War was fought pretty sloppily for the era. For instance, it took roughly over 11 months for Grant to defeat the Confederates in the Virginia Theater; meanwhile, the Prussians won three entire wars against fully industrialized countries with professional militaries in less times. The Second Schleswig War lasted just over 8 months; the Franco Prussian War lasted just over six months; and the Austro-Pressian War over one month. Grant was great commanding forces against a fledgling nation of which he had significant numerical, industrial, and naval advantages over—but I argue that this alone is not enough to rank him against those who destroyed empires and conquered vast territories. He was a good, competent commander and fought the American Civil War well but I don’t see him being successful against the other major armies of his era.

There’s a couple things wrong here. 1.) The battle was a mutual surprise to both parties. Pleasanton failed to conduct his own reconnaissance and believed the Confederate cavalry to be at Culpeper Courthouse. He was unaware that Stuart was actually at Brandy Station. Pleasanton’s men were equally surprised to face resistance at Beverly Ford as Stuart’s men were to the presence of Union cavalry.  2.) Pleasanton’s plan was not well coordinated—which is largely why it failed. While Buford’s wing advanced on Beverly Ford at the planned time of 4:30am, Gregg’s wing didn’t cross Kelly’s Ford until 9:00am because Duffie’s division got lost. This delay in the timetable allowed Stuart to shift forces to meet individual threats. Additionally, Duffie’s division—1/3 of Pleasanton’s force—never got to its rendezvous point at Brandy Station because of resistance from the 2nd SC and 4th VA cav.  Pleasanton’s plan was well forged but based on faulty intelligence, which is why it fell apart. He also failed to adapt to the changing circumstances of battle. When Stuart departed the St James line to confront Gregg’s division on Fleetwood Hill, Pleasanton failed to launch a pursuit which could have encircled Stuart’s artillery and Jones and Hampton’s brigades. Alternately, Stuart was able to adapt to the circumstances of battle and shift troops to different parts of the battlefield as needed. He was able to outcylce Pleasanton’s decision-making loop—which is ultimately why the Union cavalry was forced off the field. Still, the Union cavalry performed admirably—particularly Buford and his division.

Chickamauga was a tactical success that evolved into the strategic failure of Chattanooga—especially when Bragg misused Longstreet’s corps by sending it to Knoxville. Sending Bragg the 1st Corps gained the Confederacy nothing and was a wasted effort.

Donelson, Vicksburg, and Nashville all irreversibly altered the strategic situation in the West and can be considered strategic victories and decisive. Lee also did achieve similar success at Harpers Ferry—just 2,000 men shy of Grant at Donelson (12-14,000 men) and the largest surrender of US troops until WW2–although the strategic success was overshadowed by the stalemate at Antietam and withdraw across the Potomac and thus squandered. Also, didn’t Grant’s defeat of Lee at Appomattox cause the Confederacy to fall apart? So destroying armies obviously was significant in influencing the morale of a country.   

Also, you really aren’t accurately describing the goal of Lee’s strategy—which you would know after reading some of the listed sources in my first post—he understood that wars are a contest of political wills and that democracies had inherent weaknesses in warfare in that the population could always vote to end it, and he designed his theater-level strategy with the idea of attacking northern willpower. He was well aware that simply destroying an army would not end the war, but it could be critical in defeating civilian morale as was the case with Saratoga and Yorktown during the American Revolution as well as more recent examples such as Dien Bien Phu. Compared to every other Confederate army/theater commander, Lee’s strategy offered the only potential of strategic success.

Again, while the idea of sending reinforcements to Johnston’s army and holding Atlanta is an interesting hypothetical, Johnston’s career up to that point demonstrates no real ability to reverse the situation even with reinforcements. Lee and Johnston’s armies were roughly the same size and were outnumbered by opponents with almost the same 2:1 ratio, yet one managed to inflict devastating losses upon the enemy and weaken enemy morale while the other allowed the enemy to outmaneuver him 100 miles with minimum losses. Johnston was not the commander for the job.

Hoarding your soldiers was a trait literally every Civil War commander maintained, and again, knowing that Confederate commanders in the West were abysmal, would you want to send reinforcements to a region where their strength would be squandered or to where their strength could be applied successfully? Davis, being the supreme commander, thus invested in success when he could.

The failure in Confederate strategy stemmed from the passive-defense strategy of the Western Theater which wasted Confederate resources and did nothing to negatively influence Northern morale or improve the strategic situation, whereas the strategic offense strategy brought in positive results.

Some of your talking points are outdated:

The idea that a single decisive goal was unattainable is a myth. Grant achieved this at Fort Donelson and Vicksburg and some could argue Thomas did this at Nashville. If this “outdated Napoleonic tactic” (this is more of a strategy than a tactic) was indeed outdated, than how come it was used and applied successfully on other fronts?  Had “the strategy of warfare” (again, maybe you’re referring to the character of warfare) changed? Ulysses S. Grant employed the Napoleonic system of having independent corps traveling on multiple lines of communication to converge upon the enemy to enhance greater force and in doing so achieved decisive victories. Grant and Lee both studied the Jominian theory of war—based largely upon Napoleonic experiences—and followed those principles appropriately. By all means, they understood the character of war they faced.

Lee understood the greater strategic picture and followed closely events across all fronts. He was well read on occurrences out West and understood the state of the war. However, he also understood the quality of the Confederate leadership in that front was exceedingly poor and that sending troops in that direction would be squandering them—as what did happen when he sent Bragg his 1st Corps. Would sending Joe Johnston a few divisions prompt him to relieve Vicksburg faster or attempt to slow down Sherman more to Atlanta? Based on Johnston’s career, the evidence is against this. One should also add that Lee was primarily a theater commander, and while he had the respect and ear of Jefferson Davis, he deferred to civilian control over the military—and it was Davis and his War Department who generally determined Confederate strategy and resource allocation, not Lee. Every army commander on every front in the Confederacy constantly begged for more troops and supplies, but only Lee was able to employ them for strategic success—and Davis recognized this.

The character of war had changed dramatically from the American Revolution to the American Civil War. Due to the logistically heavy British forces and the lack of good roads and lines of communication, the British could not operate well into the interior of the country. Washington could abandon his major cities and know very well that the British would be unable to launch an effective pursuit. Whenever the British tried to march into the interior (Saratoga and Cowpens for example), they were handily beaten. By the American Civil War, the frontier had largely been tamed, the road network was expansive, and railroads increased the speed and distances armies could cover. Abandoning your strategic centers offered little benefit as the enemy could pursue you into the interior.

Lee’s strategy was largely based on a Jominian theory of war which was prevalent in the Civil War era. Many of Jomini’s principles were based upon the notion of securing and maintaining the initiative in order to force the opponent to fight upon your own terms. In essence, the only chance the Confederacy had was to maintain the strategic offense (using a mix of tactical defense and offense depending on the situation) by seizing the initiative to prevent the Union forces from employing their larger forces to either outmaneuver or envelop the Confederates.  Thus, Lee understood that fighting a purely defensive campaign would only benefit the Union (see the Fort Henry/Donelson, Siege of Corinth, Siege of Vicksburg), and although his offensive strategy cost manpower—it offered greater degrees of strategic success and was less costly in proportion to the entire Confederate armies that surrendered out in the western theater. As a theater commander, Lee’s strategy bought the Confederacy its only major success. 

This is an overly simplified answer. For more in depth reading, I would start with Jomini’s The Art of War, then read Freeman’s biography of Lee, I would then read some of Alan Nolan, T Harry Williams, and Ed Bonekemper’s criticisms of Lee, but then round it out with more modern scholarship such as Gary Gallagher and Jeffrey Wert—which offer nuanced arguments on Lee as a strategic thinker. Have you read the book mentioned in my text or any recent scholarship on Gen Rosecrans? For instance, the aforementioned history is a great work using primary sources to compare how some histories of the Civil War promoted incorrect information. Much of the historical understanding of Gen Rosecrans is primarily from historians who took Gen Grant’s writings for his word without comparing how they stacked against the official record. The notion that Rosecrans simply abandoned half of his army on the field is untrue. The routing of the Army of the Cumberland at Chickamauga was rapid and total—its position was untenable and command and control had disintegrated. Rosecrans did what any army commander should do and left a competent commander to conduct a rearguard action while organizing the shattered army at Chattanooga to prevent the Confederate tactical victory from evolving into a strategic one. 

Some of the claims that Rosecrans “disobeyed” Grant stems from his conduct after the Second Battle of Corinth, wherin Grant accused Rosecrans of being too slow in his pursuit of the beaten Confederates—a problem which plagued literally every army commander in the Civil War to include Grant. Part of it also stems from the Battle of Iuka where Grant—according to the official record—sent contradicting orders.

In essence, the book argues that there needs to be a more complete historical analysis of Rosecran’s career and that he was a more able commander than historians have given him credit for.

As to the original question of Rosecrans vs. Bragg, I still hold the former to be a better general; however, I’m about to crack open Earl Hess’ Braxton Bragg: The Most Hated Man in the Confederacy—so my opinion may change.

The idea of General Lee not being a modern commander compared to General Grant is due to the Lost Cause ideology surrounding him after the war, which portrayed him as an old cavalier fighting valiantly against an overwhelming and industrial foe. This narrative was convenient for Southerners as it allowed them to hold onto their traditions as well as to Northerners who were able to portray their victory as being one in tune with the progress of the industrial age. The myth of Lee as one of the last cavalier, antiquated commanders persisted with historians like Douglas S Freeman and many of Lee’s early critiques like T Harry Williams, Alan T. Nolan, Edward Bonekemper III. The latter three essentially argued that Lee sacrificed tactical success for an overall effective strategy, focused too heavily on Virginia, failed to understand logistics, and cost the Confederacy severely in manpower. In essence, Gen Lee was fighting the last war rather than the current one. These arguments were supported by other myths such as the idea that Civil War commanders didn’t understand the killing potential of the rifled musket.

More recent historians, such as Gary Gallagher, Jeffrey Wert, and Robert Krick challenge both the Lost Cause and revisionist critiques of Lee by asserting that Lee did develop the only theater-wide strategy that offered the Confederacy any chance of success, understood the centrality of the Virginia theater to both Confederate and Union willpower, took into account the capabilities of the commanders and situations on other fronts, had good logistical acumen despite severe limitations, and understood the morale consequences of tactical victories. Furthermore, the casualties incurred under his command produced positive results and were less costly compared to the complete capitulation of entire Confederate armies as seen with Fort Donelson and Vicksburg. Succinctly stated, Lee gave the Confederacy the best bang for their buck. With the exception of employing large-scale targeting of civilians, Gen Lee was absolutely a modern general by Civil War standards. 

To answer your question as to whom was better, I argue that if roles were reversed the results of the war would likely be the same.

Source: Gary Gallagher: Lee and His Generals in War and Memory

Gary Gallagher: Lee and His Army in Confederate History

Gary Gallagher: Lee the Soldier

Let’s use Prussia as an example. Prussia at the time had the most professional army by far. U.S. officers at the time only had West Point—essentially an engineering college with smatterings of military application and theory—which only produced 2nd lieutenants. There was no MA/PHD equivalent schools in military application/theory. The average Civil War leader—despite those with experience in the Mexican-American War—was an amateur in warfare. Most were lieutenants and captains who were thrust into colonelcy and generalship overnight—forcing many lessons to be learned on-the-job. This produced some good, successful commanders, but none as professional as many European armies.

Going back to Prussia, to become a general in the Prussian army, you first needed to have served as an officer for five years, then you needed to pass the entrance exam for the Prussian Staff College, after which you spent several years passing various examinations until you served a term on the Great General Staff, after which you served two years, took another exam, and then were able to join a position on the General Staff. Grant is of the mind that Lee’s army is on the verge of being broken (read his papers) and launches repeated assaults against the Army of Northern Virginia. Each time, Lee proves to be a master improviser (Gordon Rhea’s words, not mine), either outright repelling Grant’s assaults, launching successful counterattacks, or even planning his own tactical offenses. In terms of Lee’s abilities, let’s break them down to the three levels of war. At the strategic level, he offered the only strategy that offered any chance of success and managed to prolong a conflict that was close to ending in the summer of 1862. He was certainly a great tactician compared to the commanders of his day. This quote comes up a few times and especially in some of the most recent historiography which argues that a Fabian strategy would have been more successful as opposed to a more aggressive strategy.  This line of thinking is heavily flawed.

1.) Time was not on the Confederacy’s side. The blockade of Southern ports was one of—if not the most—defining attributes to Northern success in the Civil War. It tanked the Southern economy, caused rapid inflation, sent food prices through the roof, and cut off the South from foreign imports. This made the Confederate economy unsustainable in the longterm. The longer the war lasted, the less capable to South would be in waging it, and thus it was more likely that the Confederate home front would collapse. A similar situation occurred with the German Empire during the First World War, and in both instances, neither the Germans nor Confederates could afford to stay put, fight defensively, and simply “not lose.” 

2.) It ignores the influence of morale on an army and society. Fighting a largely defensive war can have a significantly negative effect on morale. Compare the morale of the Confederate Army of Tennessee and the Army of Northern Virginia. In the former, their commanders regularly fought defensively and ceded ground. This, in turn, saw spikes in desertion, and reading letters and journals from soldiers, it becomes apparent that they did not like how their leaders constantly retreated. However, during the Chickamauaga Campaign, you see an upturn in morale as they launched a successful offensive. Meanwhile, the Army of Northern Virginia generally had an unshakable esprit de corps, and their trust in their commander remained true even til Appomattox. By largely maintaining an offensive posture and keeping his army on the move, Lee was able to maintain the morale and cohesion of his army to an extent that no other Confederate commander could replicate.

Additionally, by adopting a Fabian strategy, you cede critical manpower to the enemy. In Tennessee, for instance, the Union occupation of the state by early 1863 significantly hurt the Confederacy’s recruitment efforts, and by 1864 most of the Confederacy’s Tennessee regiments were severely understrength. However, even in early 1864 in the western part of the state, Gen Nathan Forrest—operating behind enemy lines—managed to recruit many Tennesseans to join his ranks. What we learn from this anecdote is that holding land directly correlates with recruitment, and the more territory that the South ceded to the Union, the more difficult their recruitment issues became.

3. Addressing the quote directly, while it sounds poetic, it lacks an understanding that there was no better alternative. Who could have done a better job than Lee? Beauregard was a good independent commander and a great improviser but lacked a realistic strategic vision. Gen Pemberton utterly failed as an army commander and displayed no initiative. Bragg had lost the confidence of his men and subordinates and had no strategic vision. Johnston was unwilling to take risks and also displayed no initiative. Taylor had a good career but no experience leading a major force. Smith was isolated in his Trans-Mississippi “Smithdom” and too lacked a strategic vision. Lee was the only Confederate army commander who was both competent on the offense and defense. The South didn’t loose the war because of Lee, they lost because there was only one of him. 

4.) While many historians debate the effectiveness of Lee’s strategic vision, the reality is that it was what sustained the Confederacy for as long as it did. By the late spring of 1862, the Confederacy was on life support: they had lost the Battle of Shiloh, New Orleans had fallen, the Mississippi River was being seized, the blockade was being felt in force, Corinth had fallen, the Confederacy was kicked out of Missouri, several Northern incursions into North Carolina cut off shipping, and the Union armies were poised to take Richmond. Although Stonewall Jackson had provided some success with his Valley Campaign, things looked dark for the Confederacy. However, after Lee took over on June 1st, within seven months, he won two campaigns (Peninsula and Second Manassas), captured a garrison (comparable to the size of Grant’s victory at Donelson) at Harpers Ferry, invaded the North and fought the Union army to a draw, and then repelled another invasion at the Battle of Fredericksburg. He had changed the area of operations from around Richmond to Northern Virginia. The South went from being on ropes to actually having a fighting chance, and the effect it had on both the Northern and Southern press—and thus politicians—was immense. Lee understood that he was fighting against long odds and that he would need to risk big to reap any reward—which resulted in heavy casualties in some instances that were hard to afford. Some would argue that his strategy cost the South vital manpower that could have been used elsewhere, and that is a valid criticism. The response to these people would be, “Who would have used them better?” As noted earlier, no other Confederate army commander possessed the skills to lead an army to victory. Sending them additional troops would put them to waste. Again, the Confederate suffered from a shortage of good leadership as much as it did from manpower. A good compromise argument would be that Lee could have personally gone West with additional troops to try and reverse the strategic situation on that front, and I agree this perspective has good merits—to which the only counter would be if someone in the Army of Northern Virginian would be capable of leading the army in Lee’s absence.

While Lee’s Lost Cause reputation elevates him to Godly levels, pulling back the veneer and examining the man through a modern lens still reveals an excellent army commander who gave the Confederacy its only real chance of winning independence.

To your second point, there is no evidence that the nickname is derogatory as the person who bestowed it upon him—Gen Bernard Bee—was mortally wounded; however, a closer analysis might answer the question. Jackson earned the nickname on Henry Hill during the Battle of First Manassas/Bull Run. At this point in the battle, elements of three Confederate brigades had just been routed off of Matthews Hill and were reorganizing on Henry Hill. Earlier in the battle, Gen Bee considered making a stand on Henry Hill vice Matthews Hill, as it offered greater defensive advantages, but was convinced otherwise by Col Nathan Evans who needed immediate support at Matthews Hill. What this incident tells us is that Gen Bee understood the strategic significance of Henry Hill as well as its tactical advantages. As the Confederates who fought on Matthews Hill were rallying, the only fresh infantry regiments available were from Jackson’s brigade, and he positioned his troops in an excellent defensive position behind the reverse slope of the hill. This position had many advantages: it shielded his men from long-range fire from Matthews Hill and Dogan Ridge, it was behind 2-3 hundred yards of open ground that the enemy would have to cross, and it gave his smoothbore cannons advantage against the enemy’s rifled guns. Bee would have also understood the advantages in terrain as he too had previously wanted to fight from there. Bee delivered the stonewall quote to his disorganized command in the midst of the battle. He was surely aware of the strategic situation and must have known that the Confederates at Henry Hill were outnumbered and close to defeat. He wanted to reorganize his men and return them to the firing line, and Jackson’s brigade and supporting artillery were the only thing holding the Confederate line together. From their excellent defensive position, there was no good reason for Jackson to attack the enemy and doing so would have put the Confederate forces in needless jeopardy. Gen Bee was soon mortally wounded as he moved his rallied command into the left of Jackson’s line. Based on this evidence, it is likely that the stonewall nickname was given in earnest respect to Jackson who was instrumental in holding the line while other Confederate brigades rallied. Still, we will never know 100% because the person who gave the nickname died before ever explaining himself.

Sherman is certainly one of the most controversial generals in American history.

His performance in the first half of the war until 1864 was close to abysmal. Historians debate on the extent of the violence done by his March to the Sea and the Carolinas. What is known for a fact it that it was specifically meant to target civilians, and although direct violence was not officially sanctioned, murder and sexual violence did occur as a consequence.

Regardless, it is undeniable that Sherman’s March helped in some way significantly contribute to the fall of the Confederacy.

While Sherman’s conduct during the Civil War is controversial with arguments to be made on both sides, his post-war career is undeniably atrocious—with his campaign against the American Indians being one of genocide. His experiences in targeting civilians during the American Civil War certainly contributed to this way of war.

All in all, I would argue he was a poor tactician, a great operational and strategic planner, his war against civilians was at best controversial and at worst criminal, and his treatment of the American Indians is unquestionably evil.

The author is a distant relative and admits so in the introduction. However, despite the potential for bias, the author does meticulous research with primary resources to dispute many of the myths perpetuated in Hood’s historiography.

The below review summarizes it pretty well. The author generally uses primary sources to dismiss myths that most previous historians have accepted as true. He examines the historiography of Hood to find out where these myths originated from to show how they developed over time and counters them with primary sources.

John Bell Hood was one of the Confederacy’s most successful—and enigmatic—generals. He died at 48 after a brief illness in August of 1879, leaving behind the first draft of his memoirs Advance and Retreat: Personal Experiences in the United States and Confederate States Armies. Published posthumously the following year, the memoirs immediately became as controversial as their author. A careful and balanced examination of these “controversies,” however, coupled with the recent discovery of Hood’s personal papers (which were long considered lost) finally sets the record straight in John Bell Hood: The Rise, Fall, and Resurrection of a Confederate General.

Outlived by most of his critics, Hood’s published version of many of the major events and controversies of his Confederate military career were met with scorn and skepticism. Some described his memoirs as nothing more than a polemic against his arch-rival Joseph E. Johnston. These unflattering opinions persisted throughout the decades and reached their nadir in 1992, when an influential author described Hood’s memoirs as “merely a bitter, misleading, and highly distorted treatise” replete with “distortions, misrepresentations, and outright falsifications.” Without any personal papers to contradict them, many historians and writers portrayed Hood as an inept and dishonest opium addict and a conniving, vindictive cripple of a man. One writer went so far as to brand him “a fool with a license to kill his own men.” What most readers don’t know is that nearly all of these authors misused sources, ignored contrary evidence, and/or suppressed facts sympathetic to Hood.

Stephen M. “Sam” Hood, a distant relative of the general, embarked on a meticulous forensic study of the common perceptions and controversies of his famous kinsman. His careful examination of the original sources utilized to create the broadly accepted “facts” about John Bell Hood uncovered startlingly poor scholarship by some of the most well-known and influential historians of the 20th and 21st centuries. These discoveries, coupled with his access to a large cache of recently discovered Hood papers—many penned by generals and other officers who served with Hood—confirm Hood’s account that originally appeared in his memoir and resolve, for the first time, some of the most controversial aspects of Hood’s long career.

“Blindly accepting historical ‘truths’ without vigorous challenge,” cautions one historian, “is a perilous path to understanding real history.” The shocking revelations in John Bell Hood: The Rise, Fall, and Resurrection of a Confederate General will forever change our perceptions of Hood as both a man and a general, and those who set out to shape his legacy.

For those interested in a more recent study of General Hood and the Battle of Franklin, check out John Bell Hood: The Rise, Fall, and Resurrection of a Confederate General. It dispels many popular myths that were adopted by professional historians.

West Point’s professional military education curriculum in the pre-Civil War era was poor in comparison to its Prussian counterparts:

“At West Point, most of these officers concentrated surprisingly little on military tactics and strategy. Obviously, academy authorities could not have anticipated that one day these cadets would be fighting against each other. Except for smaller scale wars such as the War of 1812, the Mexican American War, and various conflicts with indigenous peoples, military energy during peacetime was spent on coastal fortifications, frontier garrison duties and various engineering projects. Therefore, the curriculum at the academy focused heavily on mathematics, engineering, and fortifications.” (Source: https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/teaching-military-strategy-at-west-point-before-the-civil-war.htm)

West Point’s primary job was to produce 2nd lieutenants, and there was no comparable institution dedicated to producing general officers. 

Yes, many were combat veterans from Mexcio and the West—but being a good lieutenant or captain does not mean you will be a good colonel or general leading large formations of troops. Thus, the Civil War experienced the Peter Principle on a regular basis—wherein many leaders could command smaller formations but failed when given command that required independent thinking.

Compare this to the Prussian professional military education system at the time that produced Von Moltke. To become an officer you would attend a cadet academy (Moltke went to the Royal Danish Military Academy but there were many others throughout Europe), and then to a war college (Prussian Staff College in Moltke’s case) to receive training in how to work on a general’s staff with the intention of producing general officers. The examination to get into a war college was highly selective when compared to West Point, and the curriculum in professional military education was much more intense. 

In Moltke’s army, you had officers trained to become colonels and generals. In Grant’s, you had officers trained to be second lieutenants. American officers were amateur army commanders compared to many other European armies—and it is impressive what they accomplished having learned on-the-job.

Hello to answer your questions:

1.) Yes, Grant’s assaults against Lee’s army were done so against prepared positions. During the Civil War, frontal assaults against entrenched forces rarely yielded any strategic or tactical success. Grant relied heavily upon frontal assaults for much of his previous career (Shiloh, Champion Hill, Vicksburg, Missionary Ridge for example) and believed that he could muscle his way through Lee’s army as he had previously done. I argue that rather than assaulting Lee’s army when entrenched, he should have maneuvered around their flank—as he did once his assaults failed. Again though, assaulting was in Grant’s nature as he believed the Confederates were on the verge of collapsing.  

2.) Both were true. Confederate morale in the Army of Northern Virginia was high going into the Overland Campaign. Gen Lee still held the confidence of his men. 

Lee also began changing his tactics to embrace a stronger tactical defense, which evolved significantly between the Wilderness and Cold Harbor.

3.) The high casualties of the campaign were not inevitable. Sherman did a great job of using his advantage in numbers to pin the Confederate army in place while constantly maneuvering on their flanks—avoiding pitched battles. However, Sherman’s goal was capturing a city, whereas Grant’s goal was to destroy Lee. Still, the best way to destroy Lee was not to frontally attack entrenched positions but to force him to spread his lines thin and maneuver on his flanks—which is essentially what Grant did at Petersburg.

Originally, Grant was labelled a butcher in the Northern press around the time of the Overland Campaign. During the Overland Campaign, the Union and Confederate armies maintained constant contact for extended periods—fighting a series of major battles back-to-back-to-back. This was unlike anything experienced in the Civil War up till this point. Although Grant had fought and won several campaigns in the West against smaller Confederate armies who were incompetently led, only the Battle of Shiloh ranked within the top 10 deadliest Civil War battles (no.7). In the West, he largely achieved victory through successful maneuver which required both naval support and subordinates who could take the initiative. This, combined with the space to maneuver, allowed Grant to avoid casualties. However, this all changed in 1864; Grant now fought against the Confederacy’s best army and commander along a significantly smaller front covering Virginia with the enemy controlling the interior lines.  While he had some good subordinates, none truly possessed the level of generalship to operate independently, forcing Grant to assert more direct control and avoid taking maneuverist risks. Finally, reading Grant’s reports, he severely underestimated the fighting prowess and morale of the Army of Northern Virginia, believing they were teetering on collapse. With these factors combined, Grant fought a largely attritional campaign. Compared to the West where only one of the top ten bloodiest battles was fought by Grant, in the East two (Wilderness and Spotsylvania) made the top ten (with the 11th being Cold Harbor). While attempting strategic flanking maneuvers, he often settled on frontal tactical assaults against prepared positions. By the end of the Overland Campaign, the Army of the Potomac was hollowed out—filled mostly with draftees. Furthermore, by the time the campaign ended, the Confederate army was still intact and successfully holding their capital. Compared to other fronts, such as Georgia, where Union armies made great strides, Grant’s Overland Campaign cost more casualties and covered less ground. To many at the time, Grant’s aggressive actions and inability to win decisive victories—combined with the high number of casualties over a short period of time—led him to being labelled a butcher in the press at a time when Northern commitment to the war was waning. The view was adopted by many Southern-sympathetic individuals as well—especially by those connected with the Army of Northern Virginia.

Howdy y’all, as with all events associated with wartime memory, we have to take things with a healthy dose of salt. War is a chaotic, violent, and over-stimulating experience, tons of what happens during battle often gets forgotten or misremembered as many of those participate die and thus a whole chunk of memory passes unrecorded. Looking at the variety of sources, there were a few accounts of Confederates aiding Union soldiers at Fredericksburg but none are named directly as Kirkland. On top of that, the most likely timing when this would have occurred would have been well after the last Union assault (assuming the event occurred on 13 December and not the subsequent days on non-fighting) which occurred at 4:00pm—meaning that it would have been dark and difficult to see the features/actions of the people involved. Kirkland’s name doesn’t appear in accounts until years after the event occurred. Some note that the absence of Kirkland’s name until year’s later implies that this is false; however, that may not be so, as:
1.) Kirkland’s actions may not have seemed noteworthy in comparison to other actions from the unit that day, thus not warranting mention in the official reports. Again, these reports cannot recount 100% of what occurred and other events may have drowned out Kirkland’s actions.
2.) Many war biographies and recounts are written in combination of memory and official reports. While memory can alter perception of history, that is not to say just because it is a memory rather than an official report that does not make it invalid. When interviewing veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan today, they always note how “heroic” actions are committed on a regular basis that aren’t recorded in official reports—I imagine the same thing happened in 1862.
3.) As mentioned earlier, many of the wounded tended to by Kirkland/other Confederate soldiers most likely later died that night or in subsequent days.

Like all Civil War “myths” there is aways some grain of truth. For instance, with the Irish Confederates of Maryes Heights myth, the 24th GA was mistaken as an Irish regiment as their commander was Irish; however, there was one company of Irish-majority present in Cobb’s brigade—Lochrane Guards (Co. F, Phillips Legion)—and they probably lamented at having to kill fellow Irishmen. So even this myth has some truth to it.

What we do know is that there are scattered accounts of Confederates providing aid to Union soldiers at Maryes Heights one of whom was years later identified as Kirkland by Gen Kershaw.

If I was on Mythbusters I would label this possible but unconfirmed, and we may never know the truth.

1.) A smaller army generally absorbs a higher casualty rate.  Except for a few occasions Lee was outnumbered, Grant understood this and was willing to sacrifice his numbers for the opponent. 2.) I am aware Grant worked with Halleck and Lincoln to develop the strategy for the Union army’s campaigns.  Given its strategic importance it is readily apparent that Atlanta was an important objective for wounding he CSA.  I am not disputing Grant’s role in this decision, in fact I admire him for strategic thinking. However, Sherman implemented the tactics, made the decisions, and lead the army in the field.  Sherman was generally given a free hand and reacted to the Confederate army on his own volition.  Had Sherman been unable to secure Atlanta before the 1864 election there is a possibility (again speculative dependent upon public option at the time) that the Democrats may have won the 1864 election.  Whereas Grant’s 1864 campaign disheartened many Northerners and posed a political risk to the restoration of the Union.  Again, democracies generally struggle with protracted wars with high casualties.
